The haiku’s brevity mirrors the constriction of the soul, compressing an entire season of hope and despair into seventeen syllables.

**Literary criticism:**  
From this perspective, the poem’s formal elements reinforce its theme of thwarted expectation. The anaphoric structure—the identical phrase bookending the middle line—creates a circular, trapped movement, as if the speaker cannot escape the thought of May’s failure. The grammatical ambiguity of “来ぬ” (which could also be read as the perfective “has come”) is not resolved; instead, the repetition forces both readings to coexist, generating a discordant tension between what is hoped for and what actually occurs. The poem thus critiques the naive expectation that nature’s cycles bring comfort, revealing instead how those cycles can become a source of existential dread when they fail to align with human need. The lack of any specific natural imagery (no blossoms, no rain, no moon) heightens the abstract, psychological quality of the desperation—it is not a particular feature of May that is missed, but the very idea of May’s arrival as an anchor for hope. In this reading, the haiku becomes a stark meditation on the fragility of human reliance on seasonal order.
